summaryRaw: Earlier today, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. These releases fix two critical vulnerabilities that, under the right conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems.

This post isn't about how to update. It's about how these vulnerabilities were found and fixed, what has changed in how PHP security is handled over the past two years, and what we need from the organizations that depend on PHP to keep PHP's security work going.

CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w: RCE via OOM corruption (out-of-memory): If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory. On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings. Remote code execution was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths. CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp: RCE via stale global state: A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request. A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.

Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.
A first external audit and increased security focus

comments.author: dofm
comments.textRawHtml:
You may never hear me say this again because I am a gruff cynic who is not sure that hanging out here is good for his psyche, but thank goodness for HN.

While I have been chasing around today, trying to resolve this on different servers, it turns out a three line nginx mitigation (blocking multipart uploads) I wrote in the wee small hours GMT has been quietly protecting a vulnerable machine I could not shut down (from attacks powered by every single mainstream agentic AI tool — Anthropic, OpenAI, Qwen cloud, Baidu, seemingly also AWS, Meta)

Including an hour before the PHP patch actually shipped.

So without the HN discussion I wouldn't have found enough people pointing at possible mitigations and I would have lost a server to this, and I thank everyone who pointed out that second mitigation in particular.

children.author: tasuki
children.textRawHtml:
> from attacks powered by every single mainstream agentic AI

Is it so bad? Have you measured the number of attacks?

> So without the HN discussion I wouldn't have found enough people pointing at possible mitigations and I would have lost a server to this

I run a tiny server. I like this server a lot. I only patched an hour after the Debian package was ready and didn't think about it again. Do you mean to imply there's a real chance my little server has been compromised?

[Edit:] My server is quite public too. It hosts four SLDs and many subdomains and receives both human and bot traffic. Only one or two subdomains use PHP, but a reasonable attacker surely tries all of them.

children.author: dofm
children.textRawHtml:
> Is it so bad? Have you measured the number of attacks?

It is not a torrent, no. Dozens up to hundreds, rather than hundreds to thousands.

But they would very likely have succeeded, right? It's a fairly turnkey vulnerability.

> I run a tiny server. I like this server a lot. I only patched an hour after the Debian package was ready and didn't think about it again. Do you mean to imply there's a real chance my little server has been compromised?

Can't say one way or another. Have a look at your log file for POST requests in quick succession for things like

  /_next 
  /_next/server
  /app
  /actions
  /api
  /dashboard
> [Edit:] My server is quite public too. It hosts four SLDs and many subdomains and receives both human and bot traffic. Only one or two subdomains use PHP, but a reasonable attacker surely tries all of them.

All my "obviously PHP app" domains got visited. None of my bespoke app domains (which are not obviously PHP). Though over time, the bespoke domains do get a whole bunch of boring probes for WP vulnerabilities etc., like all websites get.

Depends how your logging works. If you ingest logs to a remote server it's quite hard for an attacker to clean those up.
Also I'd guess that most of the PHP exploits tried today weren't sophisticated but rather brute force and then either cryptomining or botnetting or something like this.

children.author: dofm
children.textRawHtml:
I think it doesn't, but I have to say, I have never seen an automated attack on a PHP application that has bothered to hide its traces.

If your attacker is someone known to you, some kind of persistent threat, then maybe they would? But most of this stuff is typically kind of worm-like; attack one box, use it to attack another, move on.

With this particular server I am in two minds about whether it is likely I have any persistent type hackers, but I must say what it looks like is automated attacks. AI script kiddies, almost. These same boxes attract all the typical PHP app probes (WP2shell etc.)

And FWIW what it actually mostly looked like was hits from some sort of cloud-based AI search API; they suddenly stopped at the same time as if someone else had pulled a plug. So maybe someone running an agentic search API decided not to be part of the probes.

children.author: codebje
children.textRawHtml:
Quantity is a form of quality.

There's a vast number of operators who won't even look at their site when its performance craters due to a scrum of crypto miners all competing for resources. Why waste time on sophisticated attacks trying to fly under the radar of competent admins who will detect you by your egress traffic anyway?
